function_statements.text: A type II topoisomerase that negatively supercoils closed circular double-stranded (ds) DNA in an ATP-dependent manner to maintain chromosomes in an underwound state, while in the absence of ATP it relaxes supercoiled dsDNA (PubMed:15047530, PubMed:16377674, PubMed:16876125, PubMed:18426901, PubMed:19060136, PubMed:19596812, PubMed:20805881, PubMed:22844097). Also catalyzes the interconversion of other topological isomers of dsDNA rings, including catenanes (PubMed:16876125, PubMed:19060136, PubMed:22457352). Gyrase from M.tuberculosis has higher decatenation than supercoiling activity compared to E.coli; as M.tuberculosis only has 1 type II topoisomerase, gyrase has to fulfill the decatenation function of topoisomerase IV as well (PubMed:16876125, PubMed:22457352, PubMed:23869946). At comparable concentrations M.tuberculosis gyrase cannot introduce as many negative supercoils into DNA as the E.coli enzyme, and its ATPase activity is lower, perhaps because it does not couple DNA wrapping and ATP binding as well as E.coli (PubMed:22457352, PubMed:24015710)

Negative supercoiling favors strand separation, and DNA replication, transcription, recombination and repair, all of which involve strand separation. Type II topoisomerases break and join 2 DNA strands simultaneously in an ATP-dependent manner

BACKGROUND: Fluoroquinolones (FQs) are potential drugs that inhibit DNA synthesis and are used in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) and short-term anti-TB regimens. In recent years, a high proportion of FQ resistance has been observed in Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates. The development of FQ resistance in multidrug-resistant TB negatively impacts patient treatment outcome and is a serious threat to control of TB. METHODS: The study included a total of 562 samples from patients with pulmonary TB that had been on anti-tuberculosis therapy. MTBDRsl assays were performed for the molecular detection of mutations. Sequence analysis was performed for the characterization and mutational profiling of FQ-resistant isolates. RESULTS: FQ resistance was observed in 104 samples (18.5%), most of which were previously treated and treatment failure cases. A total of 102 isolates had mutations in DNA gyrase subunit A (gyrA), while mutations in gyrB were observed in only two isolates. Mutational analysis revealed that the mutations mostly alter codons 94 (replacing aspartic acid with glycine, D94G) and 90 (replacing alanine with isolates had mutations in DNA gyrase subunit A (gyrA), while mutations in gyrB were observed in only two isolates. Mutational analysis revealed that the mutations mostly alter codons 94 (replacing aspartic acid with glycine, D94G) and 90 (replacing alanine with valine, A90V). In MDR and treatment failure cases, resistance to FQs was most commonly associated with the D94G mutation. In contract, a high proportion of A90V mutations were observed in isolates that were newly diagnosed. CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that genotypic assays for FQ resistance should be carried out at the time of initial diagnosis, before starting treatment, in order to rule out mutations that impact the potential use of FQs in treatment and to control drug resistance.

New classes of drugs are needed to treat tuberculosis (TB) in order to combat the emergence of resistance (MDR and XDR) to existing agents and shorten the duration of therapy. Mycobacterial DNA gyrase B subunit has been identified to be one of the potentially under exploited drug targets in the field of antitubercular drug discovery. In the present review, we discussed the synthesis, structural optimization and docking study of effective potent DNA gyrase inhibitor against M. tuberculosis, with improved properties such as enhanced activity against MDR strains, reduced toxicity. Based on this progress, if we can successfully leverage the opportunities in this target, there is hope that we will be able to raise novel gyrase inhibitor in earnest in the long.

summary:
## gyrB (Rv0005, mtu) — DNA gyrase subunit B

### Function

UniProt has a **reviewed, experimentally supported** entry: **P9WG45** (GYRB_MYCTU, locus tag Rv0005), "DNA gyrase subunit B". Its function statement carries experimental evidence (ECO:0000269) and describes:

- P9WG45 "A type II topoisomerase that negatively supercoils closed circular double-stranded (ds) DNA in an ATP-dependent manner to maintain chromosomes in an underwound state, while in the absence of ATP it relaxes supercoiled dsDNA"
- A distinctive mycobacterial feature: P9WG45 "Gyrase from M.tuberculosis has higher decatenation than supercoiling activity compared to E.coli; as M.tuberculosis only has 1 type II topoisomerase, gyrase has to fulfill the decatenation function of topoisomerase IV as well" — i.e. this is a hybrid gyrase/topo IV enzyme, and it is also comparatively weak: P9WG45 "At comparable concentrations M.tuberculosis gyrase cannot introduce as many negative supercoils into DNA as the E.coli enzyme, and its ATPase activity is lower".
- Catalytic activity: "ATP-dependent breakage, passage and rejoining of double-stranded DNA."
- Subunit / division of labour within the holoenzyme: P9WG45 "Heterotetramer, composed of two GyrA and two GyrB chains (PubMed:15047530). In the heterotetramer, GyrA contains the active site tyrosine that forms a transient covalent intermediate with DNA, while GyrB binds cofactors and catalyzes ATP hydrolysis" — GyrB is the ATPase/energy-transducing subunit.

The single-type-II-topoisomerase point is independently reflected in the corpus: PMID:23869946 "In contrast with most bacteria which possess two type II topoisomerases (topoisomerase IV and DNA gyrase), Mycobacterium tuberculosis possesses only one, DNA gyrase, which is functionally a hybrid enzyme."

Two further UniProt entries matched the symbol, **E5G958** and **A9X5B9**, but both are unreviewed and, per the tool note, hold no FUNCTION statement — nothing to draw from them beyond the same catalytic-activity line.

Structural coverage is extensive: PDB entries listed on P9WG45 include 2ZJT, 3IG0, 3ZKB, 5BS8, 6GAU, 7UGW and 9FOY among others.

### Pathways

**KEGG is the silent source here, not biology.** KEGG resolved the symbol to `mtu:Rv0005` and returned zero pathway assignments, with the explicit note that "The gene exists in KEGG but is not mapped to any pathway in this organism." That is an annotation gap: the UniProt record above establishes the enzymatic role (DNA topology maintenance / ATP-dependent type II topoisomerase activity) with experimental evidence. I have no specific KEGG pathway ID to cite and will not invent one.

### Notable interaction partners (STRING, taxon 83332, Rv0005)

Partners with support **beyond** textmining:

| Partner | STRING ID | Combined | Strongest non-textmining channel |
|---|---|---|---|
| gyrA | 83332.Rv0006 | 0.999 | experimental 0.981, coexpression 0.941, neighbourhood 0.83 |
| mfpA | 83332.Rv3361c | 0.997 | experimental 0.997 (textmining only 0.299) |
| Rv0730 | 83332.Rv0730 | 0.956 | experimental 0.818, coexpression 0.725 |
| recF | 83332.Rv0003 | 0.975 | neighbourhood 0.726, coexpression 0.65 |
| dnaN | 83332.Rv0002 | 0.952 | neighbourhood 0.713 |

- **gyrA (83332.Rv0006)** is the biologically meaningful partner and the only one corroborated by the curated record: it is the other half of the A₂B₂ heterotetramer per P9WG45.
- **mfpA (83332.Rv3361c)** is striking because it is driven almost entirely by the experimental channel (0.997) with low textmining — a genuinely non-literature-derived link. My corpus search did not retrieve an MfpA–gyrase paper, so I can describe the evidence only as STRING's experimental channel and make no mechanistic claim about it.
- **recF (Rv0003)** and **dnaN (Rv0002)** score largely on genomic neighbourhood and coexpression — they are immediate chromosomal neighbours of Rv0005 in the conserved *dnaA-dnaN-recF-gyrB-gyrA* origin-proximal cluster, so this is operon/synteny signal, not evidence of physical contact.

Partners supported **essentially by textmining alone** (`evidence_beyond_textmining: false`), per the tool's own note: rpoB (83332.Rv0667), inhA (83332.Rv1484), embB (83332.Rv3795), rpoC (83332.Rv0668), pncA (83332.Rv2043c), recA (83332.Rv2737c), tlyA (83332.Rv1694), katG (83332.Rv1908c), groEL2 (83332.Rv0440), secA1 (83332.Rv3240c). These are the canonical drug-resistance genes co-mentioned with gyrB in resistance-survey papers; the score reflects co-citation, not interaction. Note that literature and this channel are one evidence class — e.g. PMID:25816236 is exactly the kind of paper generating it ("we conducted a systematic review... of all published studies evaluating Mycobacterium tuberculosis mutations associated with resistance to fluoroquinolones"), so citing it would not corroborate the STRING edge independently.

### Lineage marker

**Negative.** `lineage_markers` found no lineage-defining position falling within gyrB in the TB-Profiler tbdb barcode; the tool notes that 855 of 4,008 H37Rv genes carry one, so this is an informative negative. An association involving gyrB is therefore not obviously confounded by population structure at this locus — though that still needs testing against genotype data rather than being settled by this lookup.

### Drug-resistance catalogue

gyrB **is resistance-associated** at the gene level, for **levofloxacin and moxifloxacin**. Of 1,126 catalogued variants: 4 "Assoc w R", 12 "Assoc w R - Interim", 13 "Not assoc w R", 424 "Not assoc w R - Interim", 665 "Uncertain significance", 8 ungraded. The associated variants cluster in the GyrB quinolone-resistance-determining region — e.g. `tbdb:gyrB:p.Asn499Asp`, `tbdb:gyrB:p.Asn499Thr`, `tbdb:gyrB:p.Asp461Asn` (all "Assoc w R", levofloxacin) and `tbdb:gyrB:p.Glu501Asp` ("Assoc w R", moxifloxacin), with `tbdb:gyrB:p.Ser447Phe`, `tbdb:gyrB:p.Asp461His`, `tbdb:gyrB:p.Glu501Val` and `tbdb:gyrB:p.Ala504Val` graded interim. Several moxifloxacin records carry the comment "Low-level resistance (multiple, genetically linked low-level resistance mutations are additive and confer high-level resistance)".

Two cautions: this flag is about the **gene**, not about any particular gyrB variant — the majority of catalogued gyrB variants are graded "Uncertain significance" (665) or not associated. And clinically, gyrB is the minor partner: PMID:32393213 reports "A total of 102 isolates had mutations in DNA gyrase subunit A (gyrA), while mutations in gyrB were observed in only two isolates."

### Summary

gyrB encodes the ATPase subunit of M. tuberculosis DNA gyrase, the organism's sole type II topoisomerase, which must serve both the supercoiling role of gyrase and the decatenation role of topoisomerase IV. Its one well-supported physical partner is GyrA, with which it forms the A₂B₂ holoenzyme; MfpA is a strong experiment-channel link whose mechanism I cannot substantiate from the sources retrieved here. KEGG assigns it no pathway, which is an annotation gap rather than a lack of knowledge. It carries no lineage-defining barcode position, and it is a WHO-catalogued fluoroquinolone resistance gene.
